source_document.body:
Truck cameras long served fleets after a crash, as evidence to reconstruct what happened and size up their exposure in court. Carriers including Werner Enterprises now use that AI-powered video and telematics data to spot risky driving and coach it out before a crash.
Executives from Werner and Bennett Family of Companies described the shift last month on a Motive-hosted panel at the American Trucking Associations’ Management Conference & Exhibition in Charlotte, North Carolina. Austin Henderson is vice president of innovation and engineering at Werner, which bought dedicated carrier FirstFleet for $245 million in January . Jared Whitson is senior director of safety and compliance at Bennett. Both fleets use Motive’s AI platform technology.
“When I started this process, it was, OK, well, how do we do accident reconstruction? How do we know what our exposure is in the case of litigation?” Henderson said of his fleet’s camera program. “That quickly has evolved into how do we prevent the litigation?”
Prevention means reading the signals drivers send through telemetry and on-road events, he said, so the fleet can retrain a driver or, in some cases, separate from one.
“If we’re not leveraging the AI, you can rest assured that plaintiff’s attorneys know how to leverage the AI,” Henderson said.
The concern is showing up in carrier survey data. Motor carriers ranked lawsuit abuse reform as their top concern in the American Transportation Research Institute’s 2026 Critical Issues in the Trucking Industry report , released Oct. 18. Across all respondents, lawsuit abuse held the No. 2 spot for a second straight year, behind fuel prices .
In-cab alerts reach drivers in real time
Gary Johnson, Motive’s head of safety and compliance strategy, moderated the panel. In the older model, he said, a camera captured video and the back office reviewed it later. Motive’s approach for what it calls physical AI is AI-powered detection and intervention in real time, with people still overseeing the system.
Henderson’s fleet runs only outward-facing cameras. He said Motive built a distracted-driving alert that works from those cameras alone, at the fleet’s request. When it fires, the driver gets an alert in the cab, the back office gets one too, and staff call the driver to direct him to a safe place.
One driver his team brought to a safety stop called back the next day after watching the video. “You may have saved my life, because I was not aware of what was happening,” the driver said, according to Henderson.
Video clears a driver who initially opposed it
The same footage protects drivers who are not at fault. Henderson described a driver with about 20 years and 2 million miles who was “quite antagonistic about the cameras being installed.”
Two weeks after the camera went in, the driver was involved in a highway incident that the replay showed was not his fault.
“Two days later, he gets served. Two days later after that, we get notice,” Henderson said. “That takes about four days to resolve because the driver was clearly in the right.”
That driver now appears in the fleet’s training videos, telling other drivers he initially opposed the cameras and showing them what happened.
Coaching moves to the same day
At Henderson’s fleet, drivers cannot move forward in their workflow until they watch the video of a flagged event. He said around like 97% of those videos are reviewed the day they occur.
“So that means the driver’s not waiting a week, two weeks to go with a coach to work through a stop sign they ran two weeks ago,” Henderson said. “If that’s your process, that’s way too long.”
The coaching is partly automated. The fleet has loaded AI avatars of its regional safety managers into Motive’s coaching tool and tells drivers the videos are AI-produced. Henderson said he got one himself the morning of the panel, on a close-following event from the week before.
“Good drivers really want to be great drivers,” he said. “They don’t want to be caught tailgating.”
Compliance review drops to seconds
At Bennett, Whitson described the change in the compliance office. Researching a single hours-of-service event used to take four or five minutes to decide whether it was a violation. AI now delivers a recommendation with its reasoning, and staff confirm it or reject it.
“So it’s taking that [review] down from four or five minutes per event to literally 30 seconds maybe,” Whitson said.
He said he does not expect much realignment on the compliance floor at first. Staff will “get to the things that they haven’t been able to get to for a long time that just fell off the edge,” he said.
Bennett has also tied fault codes to its shops. When a truck with a critical fault code crosses a geofence at one of them, the system sends a notification. Whitson said a future version could set up the repair or work order itself. For now, Bennett’s first Motive AI Agents only notify staff .
Legacy systems slow the rollout
But challenges remain. Asked for an example of AI acting on the road, Whitson said Bennett is “not that far down that road.”
Whitson cautioned against “the blind acceptance and just going all in.”
“It has to earn our trust, and it has to keep our trust,” he said.
Henderson said older systems on both the Werner and FirstFleet sides limit how quickly new tools can be wired together.
“Plumbing’s really boring until it doesn’t work,” he said.
Both executives said smaller carriers could have an edge because they have less legacy technology to drag forward. Two years ago, Whitson said, a small fleet would have lacked the resources for projects like these.
“I would say you could have a 25-truck fleet. You could have a two-person office,” Whitson said. “And you could run that office like it’s staffed by 20 people at this point.”
Henderson’s advice for a small carrier is to “pick a provider and lean in as hard as you can.”
“I promise you, in five years, it’s going to look drastically different than it does right now,” he said. “We’re probably going to have conversations that we didn’t even imagine were possible.”
Why it matters: Truck AI dash cams used to help fleets reconstruct crashes and size their lawsuit exposure. Werner and Bennett are now using the same data from Motive for same-day coaching and real-time alerts. It’s now a difference between defending a claim and preventing the crash that triggers it.
